Chronology 1 — Creation

Part III walks the shared storyline from creation to the end. At each stage: the Bible's text, the Qur'an's text, where they converge, where they collide, then a present/weigh/judge verdict. The recurring finding will be that one continuous theological seam — God's nature → sin → forgiveness → Christ → the end — runs through every episode.

The Bible's text

  • Genesis 1: creation in six days, ordered — light (1); sky/ firmament (2); land, sea, plants (3); sun, moon, stars (4); fish, birds (5); land animals and humankind, male and female (6); God rests (7), hallowing the Sabbath (Gen 2:2–3).
  • Genesis 2: a second, differently-ordered account — the man formed first from dust, then the garden, then animals, then woman from his side.
  • Creation is by divine speech ("And God said… and it was so"); the NT reads this as creation from nothing (Heb 11:3; John 1:3; Col 1:16).

The Qur'an's text

  • Creation in six "days" (ayyam, periods): Q 7:54; 10:3; 25:59.
  • By sheer command: "Be — and it is" (kun fayakun, Q 2:117; 36:82).
  • Heavens and earth were a joined mass, then parted (Q 21:30); the heaven "expanded" (Q 51:47).
  • Humankind from clay / dust / a drop (Q 15:26; 22:5; 32:7–9); Adam taught "the names" (Q 2:31); the angels prostrate to Adam, Iblis refuses (Q 2:34).
  • A breakdown in Q 41:9–12 lists earth in 2 + sustenance in 4 + heavens in 2 — read additively this looks like eight, the classic 6-vs-8 exegetical crux (resolved by traditional exegetes as overlapping, not additive, periods).

Convergence

Six creative periods; a single God creating by fiat, with no rival deity and no pre-existent co-creator; humankind formed from earth/ clay; a primordial couple; a tempter figure.

Collision

  1. Internal Genesis tension: Gen 1 (plants day 3, before the sun day 4; humans last) vs. Gen 2 (man before plants and animals) — a well-known source-critical seam in the Bible itself.
  2. The Qur'an's 6-vs-8 arithmetic of Q 41:9–12 — an internal exegetical knot, paralleling Genesis's internal knot.
  3. Does God rest? Gen 2:2–3 has God resting on the seventh day. Q 50:38 states creation occurred "and no fatigue touched Us" — which reads naturally as a deliberate correction of Genesis. This is a genuine theological divergence, not a copying detail: it flows straight from the nature-of-God contrast (absolute transcendence vs. an anthropomorphic-friendly text).

The creation of the human being — and "Let Us make man"

What God says and does

  • Gen 1:26–28: "Let Us make man in Our image (ṣelem), after Our likeness (demut)" → then v.27 immediately shifts to the singular: "So God created man in His image… male and female He created them"; v.28 the blessing and mandate (be fruitful, fill, subdue, have dominion).
  • Gen 2:7: God forms man from dust and breathes the breath of life; 2:18 "not good that the man should be alone"; the woman from his side (2:21–23).
  • The same plural recurs: Gen 3:22 ("become like one of Us") and Gen 11:7 ("let Us go down").

The plural "Us" — read logically, all options on the table

  1. Divine council — God addressing the heavenly host (cf. Job 38:7; 1 Kgs 22:19; Isa 6:8). A mainstream academic reading; difficulty: man bears God's image, not the angels'.
  2. Plural of self-deliberation — a rhetorical cohortative, God taking counsel with Himself.
  3. Plural of majesty ("royal We") — popular, but linguistically contested: a majestic plural on the verb is not clearly attested this way in Biblical Hebrew.
  4. Trinitarian reading — intra-divine plurality, supported only retrospectively by the NT (John 1:3; Col 1:16; the Spirit in Gen 1:2).

Textual note: Elohim is grammatically a plural form but governs a singular verb (baraʾ) — understood as intensive/majestic naming, not polytheism. The v.26-plural → v.27-singular shift is the crux.

The Qur'an's "We" — and the symmetry test

The Qur'an pervasively has God say "We created man" (Q 15:26; 23:12–14; 32:7–9), alternating with "I" in the Adam scene (Q 2:30 "I am placing a khalifa"; Q 15:29 / 38:72 "I breathed into him of My spirit"). In Islamic doctrine this "We" is unambiguously the plural of majesty (taʿẓim), explicitly not plurality of persons (tawhid).

The decisive symmetry point: if the Qur'an's "We" is accepted as a majestic/non-personal plural, then that same option is fully available for Genesis's "Us." By the dossier's symmetry rule (Methodology §3), "Let Us make man" is therefore suggestive only within the cumulative case of cap. 05 — not a stand-alone proof of the Trinity.

The real divergence about the human: imago Dei vs. khalifa

  • Bible: humankind in the image of God (imago Dei) — maximal dignity, representation of God on earth.
  • Qur'an: no "image of God"; instead khalifa (vicegerent), an innate upright nature (fiṭra), and God's breathed spirit. (A ḥadith "Adam in His image" exists, but it is tradition, not Qurʾan, and its pronoun referent is disputed among scholars — flagged as tradition.)

This is the substantive seam at the creation of humanity, and it feeds directly into cap. 11 — the Fall.

Arbiter verdict — creation

Present. Both: one God, six periods, creation by command, man from earth. Bible adds Sabbath rest and a two-account structure; Qur'an adds "join-then-part" and the kun fayakun formula.

Weigh.

  • Symmetric weakness: each text carries an internal ordering/number puzzle (Genesis's two accounts; the Qur'an's 6-vs-8). Neither can use it against the other without conceding its own (Methodology §3).
  • Real divergence: the "God rests" vs. "no fatigue" point is substantive and textual, and Q 50:38 looks corrective by design.
  • Interpretively open: "Let Us make man" admits four serious readings; the Trinitarian one is retrospective, and the Qur'an's majestic "We" proves a non-personal plural is natural — so by symmetry it is not a stand-alone Trinity proof.
  • Substantive: imago Dei vs. khalifa/fiṭra is the real divergence about what the human is.
  • Out of remit: concordance with modern cosmology/biology is argued apologetically on both sides; the arbiter does not rule on science- vs-text harmonization (Methodology §5).

Judge. On the shared frame: a draw — strikingly similar. On the internal puzzles: a draw — both have one. On "does God rest": a clean divergence, with the Qur'an's wording functioning as an explicit revision of Genesis; which portrayal is "better" depends on the prior theology-of-God premise already shown to be non-arbitrable (cap. 09). On "Let Us make man": by the even-handed symmetry rule it is suggestive, not probative — the Qur'an's majestic "We" shows the plural alone settles nothing. On the human being itself: imago Dei vs. khalifa/fiṭra is a genuine divergence, internally coherent on each side, and it is what carries the seam into the Fall. The seam appears immediately.
